name: Umar Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy brake pads, filters and batteries for Redline Auto Parts, a distributor that supplies about 200 garages. I came in from a garage parts counter four years ago, so I know what mechanics grumble about, but I'm still learning the buying side. A day is checking stock levels, haggling with two or three importers, and sorting out wrong parts that came in the wrong box. I like the haggling. What wears me out is the returns pile, which never gets smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, no big deal, and carry on. If a tool saves me an hour on catalogue lookups, good, and if not, I'm not losing sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd feel fairly safe. Redline is steady, the garages always need parts, and I've got about five months of savings. The one thing that nags me is being the junior, but I've been the junior for four years and nobody's said a word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and try one or two of the tools the other buyers are using once they've proven themselves. I'd keep the savings where they are and keep paying a bit extra on the car loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I mean, it's work, so there's always something, but nothing that keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Ngozi's job mean for how you think about risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wife Ngozi's a nurse at the district hospital, and that wage is steady and will be till she retires. So I don't have to carry the whole thing alone. That lets me be a bit relaxed about my own job, and I know I'm lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about work that would still bother you in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my back. Eight hours at a desk and a stockroom in between, at 58, it isn't the AI that gets me, it's the lifting and the chair. A couple of years more and I'd like to ease down.

say: I'd say **no big deal**; a tool that saves an hour on lookups is good.
I'd tell colleagues I'm not losing **sleep** over it.
think: Redline is **steady** and garages always need parts.
I have about five months saved and nobody has complained that I'm the **junior**.
do: Try one or two tools **after** other buyers prove them.
Pay a bit **extra** on the car loan.
feel: **Calm**; there is always something at work, but nothing that keeps me up.
S0.quote: My wife Ngozi's a nurse at the district hospital, and that wage is steady and will be till she retires.
fieldNote: Calm rests on a **second steady income**, which he admits is luck.
Only real physical worry is his **back**, not AI.
Wants to **ease down** within a couple of years.

steps.text: Keep buying brake and filter stock the usual way
Pay an extra 100 pounds a month on the car loan
Wait for other buyers to prove a tool before trying it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a fair change, and the best thing is to see which tools work. I'd tell the lads on the counter that the catalogue side will go to software before the phone side does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be a little uneasy. Software is already suggesting the stock orders, and the senior buyers will be the ones using it best. As the junior, I'm the one who might be left with the dull jobs, or without a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the system properly, a few evenings a month, and ask the senior buyer Tomasz if I could shadow him. I'd also keep up my contacts with the importers, since a name on a phone still counts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert. Not frightened, just awake to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your work do you think a computer would do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The catalogue matching, definitely. Finding which filter fits which engine is something it'll do in a second, and I've spent four years memorising it. A pity, but there it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your manager about the junior buyers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't just count heads, count what people know. A junior who knows the garages and the mechanics is worth more than one who knows only the screen. I'd say that and hope it lands.

say: I'd say it's a fair change, and the best move is to see which tools **work**.
I'd tell the counter lads the **catalogue** side goes first.
think: Software already suggests stock orders, and seniors will use it **best**.
As the junior I could be left with the dull jobs, or **no job**.
do: Learn the system properly a few **evenings** a month.
Ask Tomasz, the senior buyer, if I can **shadow** him.
feel: **Alert**, not frightened, just awake to it.
S1.quote: A junior who knows the garages and the mechanics is worth more than one who knows only the screen.
fieldNote: Expects **catalogue matching** to go first, after four years memorising it.
Ngozi's wage makes this a **manageable** worry, and he knows the cushion is partly luck.

steps.text: Spend a few evenings a month learning the ordering system
Ask Tomasz to let me shadow his buying calls
Keep my importer and garage contacts up to date

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is serious and people should take it seriously. I'd say we need clear rules about who is responsible when a machine makes a buying mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my desk is gone in two or three years, and that could be before Ngozi retires. We'd live on her wage and what I've saved, about five months. It would be tight but not a disaster, since the mortgage is nearly paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use these two years to get a different job while I still have one. I'd start asking garages I know if they need a parts counter hand, because a person who knows the stock still gets hired. And I'd use every AI tool I can to look good while I'm doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd manage. I've been through short-time work before, back in 2009.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Ngozi's position change your plan if you lose the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut the holidays and the takeaways, and I'd take whatever work I could find. Ngozi says her hospital pension is protected, which helps. I'd rather work for less than sit at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a role where your counter experience matters more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A garage counter, a parts shop, even delivery driving for a while. The counter experience is the one thing I've got that AI doesn't. In two years I'd be wanting to be on that side.

say: I'd say this is **serious** and people should treat it that way.
I'd say we need clear rules on who is **responsible** for machine buying mistakes.
think: My desk is gone in two or three years, possibly before Ngozi **retires**.
We could live on her wage and my **five months** saved, since the mortgage is nearly paid.
do: Ask garages I know about a parts **counter** job while I still have this one.
Use every AI tool I can to look **good** meanwhile.
feel: **Anxious**, but I'd manage; I got through short-time work in 2009.
S2.quote: A person who knows the stock still gets hired.
fieldNote: Turns to the **counter** job because it's hands-on and customer-facing.
Draws on 2009 **short-time** work as proof he can cope.
Spouse's hospital **pension** gives him room to move.

steps.text: Ask local garages about a parts counter job
Use AI tools daily so my buying skills look current
Cut takeaways and holidays to protect savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the right pace for something this big. I'd say five years is enough for the firms to plan, and not enough for them to be sloppy about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel better. I'd be 63, close enough to the finish line that I could taper off. I'd say my job is at risk only in the last couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first two years to learn the buying software and ask for a permanent senior role, then plan to stop at 62 or 63. I'd also keep up with the garage contacts as insurance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, a little relieved. It's close enough to see but far enough to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would five years change what you'd do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a proper retraining grant and a pension that doesn't penalise stopping at 62. Nothing fancy. The old rules say 66 and I can't see my back lasting that long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the government in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whichever bit applies. A plan that's honest about older workers, because we're the ones who get missed. And please no slogans.

say: I'd say five years is the **right pace** for something this big.
I'd say it's enough time to plan, but not enough to be **sloppy**.
think: I'd feel **better**, at 63 and close to the finish line.
My job is at risk only in the **last couple** of years.
do: Learn the buying software and ask for a **permanent senior** role.
Plan to stop at **62 or 63** and keep garage contacts as insurance.
feel: A little **uneasy**, a little relieved; close enough to see, far enough to plan.
S3.quote: The old rules say 66 and I can't see my back lasting that long.
fieldNote: Back pain makes **early retirement** a realistic goal.
Asks for an honest plan for **older workers**, who he says are the ones who get missed.
Dislikes **slogans** and wants a plain, practical plan for people his age.

steps.text: Learn the buying software and ask for a senior title
Plan to stop work at 62 or 63
Keep garage counter contacts warm as a fallback

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's plenty of time, so let's not panic. I'd say the useful thing is to talk about it calmly and plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's a non-issue. I'd be 68 and retired, and my back would thank me. If I'm honest, my worry is our son Chidi, who's a few years into a logistics job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working until about 64 or 65, then retire. I'd keep saving a modest amount each month, and help Chidi if I can. In the meantime I'd keep using the tools and not make a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Ten years is a long runway and I'd be off it before the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the ten years change how you spend the next one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Chidi that logistics is going to change, and to learn the part of the work that needs a person. Warehouses are the hands-on bit, so he has a few extra years, but not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell younger buyers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the tools, but learn the people too. The importer who picks up your call at seven in the morning is worth more than any cheaper price on a screen.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty** of time, so let's not panic.
I'd say the useful move is to **plan** calmly.
think: For me it's a **non-issue**; I'd be 68 and retired.
My worry is our son Chidi, a few years into a **logistics** job.
do: Work until about **64 or 65**, then retire.
Save a **modest** amount monthly and help Chidi if I can.
feel: **Calm**; ten years is a long runway and I'd be off it before the end.
S4.quote: The importer who picks up your call at seven in the morning is worth more than any cheaper price on a screen.
fieldNote: Calm for himself, but **protective** of his son and his future.
Warehouse work gives Chidi **extra years**, which Umar reasons through.
Values **relationships** over price, which fits a man from the counter.

steps.text: Keep buying at Redline until I'm 64 or 65
Save a modest amount each month toward retirement
Advise my son Chidi on moving into hands-on logistics work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two year one worries me most, because I'd be 60 with a desk that might vanish and a back that won't take a warehouse. Ngozi's wage would carry us, which is luck. What would help is retraining that's practical, a fair early pension, and people being honest early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that being the junior at 58 is odd, and nobody asks what it means. I came in late, learned fast, and I'd like some credit for not complaining.

headlineQuote: I came in late, learned fast, and I'd like some credit for not complaining.
portrait: Umar is a **58-year-old** junior buyer of car parts, up from a garage counter four years ago.
His wife Ngozi is a **hospital nurse** with a steady wage, so the household feels more secure.
Centre in outlook and steady, he'll use AI tools **once proven** and doesn't blame anyone.
He has about **five months** saved, a bad back, and a plan to ease down at 62 or 63.
He moves from calm to anxious only in the **two year** case, and turns to a garage counter job.
biggestWorry: The **two year** picture, with a vanishing desk and a back that can't take warehouse work.
whatWouldHelp: Practical **retraining**, a fair early pension and honest early warning.
